facts.fact: Name for the term: "Đa dạng hình thái theo giới tính"
Name for the term: "khác biệt theo giới tính"
Name for the term: "sự khác biệt giới tính"
Name for the term: "Sexual Dimorphism"
How hard it is to tell a fish's sex depends on whether the sexes look visibly different.
In some species the males are larger and showier, with more striking colours, than the females.
Many aquarium species show little visible difference between males and females, so a fish's sex matters mainly to breeders.
In fish, sex can be set by chromosomes (genotypic) or by the environment (environmental).
Some freshwater species, as well as a number of reef fish, may change sex during their lifetime.
Sexing livebearers is usually easy: males are generally larger and have larger, longer, more ornate and more colourful fins than females.
In livebearers, the male's anal fin is shaped like a rod (gonopodium) and the female's like a fan; fertilisation is internal.
Male guppies (Poecilia reticulata) have a stick-like modified anal fin called a gonopodium under the belly; females are larger, less colourful and have a fan-shaped anal fin.
Adult male cá bảy màu (guppy, Poecilia reticulata) are only about 1.5 to 3.5 cm long; females are clearly larger, about 3 to 6 cm, with rounder bellies.
In female guppies (Poecilia reticulata), a dark spot near the anus called the gravid spot darkens when the female is pregnant.
In guppies (Poecilia reticulata), females are 2.5–4 cm long and males 2–3 cm.
In guppies (Poecilia reticulata), a dark area near the anus called the gravid spot appears on females after fertilisation.
Young guppies (Poecilia reticulata) can be sexed at about 4 to 6 weeks, when they begin to show colour, so males and females can be split into separate tanks.
In many female lines of guppy (Poecilia reticulata) the females are silvery grey, but in high-end lines such as Full Red and Koi the females also colour up well.
Female betta (Betta) show a small white spot on the belly, the ovipositor ('vòi trứng'); males have none.
Betta (Betta) begin to show signs of maturing at 2–3 months old; the page applies adult sexing features to fish 4 months and older.
Male betta (Betta) have long, large dorsal, anal and tail fins; females have short, neat fins and swim more heavily.
Male betta (Betta) have longer, larger and stiffer anal fins and larger, more pointed ventral fins than females.
Male betta (Betta) are usually more brightly and variably coloured than females.
Female Osteogaster aenea (bronze cory) tend to grow larger, and mature females are noticeably rounder and broader-bodied than males, especially when gravid.
Male cichlids (Cichlidae) are usually brighter and have pointed dorsal and anal fins; in many species the male's anal fin carries egg spots.
Some male cichlids (Cichlidae) develop a nuchal hump, larger in dominant males; females may grow a smaller hump when breeding.
Cyprinids are hard to sex; males are generally darker and slimmer, and in some species males show white breeding tubercles in spawning season.
In tetras, females are larger and fuller-bodied, while males have longer fins and usually brighter colours.
Catfish are generally not sexable by sight; in Corydoras, females have larger, fuller bodies than males.
In Cyclocheilichthys apogon (cá ba kỳ đỏ), body shape, external colour and fin ray counts are alike in both sexes, yet females are larger than males.
In Cyclocheilichthys apogon, females have deeper bodies and shorter but wider, deeper heads; males have a longer dorsal fin and a longer anal fin base.
In some fish, lower temperatures produce more females and higher temperatures more males; this works best with juvenile fish.
In Apistogramma, higher pH values produced more females, and water kept at about 78°F (26°C) gave the most even sex ratios.
In killifish, soft water (pH 6.5, 30 ppm hardness) at 72° to 76°F (22 to 24°C) resulted in 90 percent females.
Aphyosemion gabunense raised at pH 5.0 gave more females; Epiplatys dageti gave more females in soft water and more males in hard water.
Crowded Nothobranchius fry are reported to give larger numbers of males.
Pesticides and herbicides may mimic sex hormones, delaying sexual maturity in males and disrupting breeding.
Differences in body shape between the sexes of Cyclocheilichthys apogon may relate to spawning and movement behaviour.

To sex young betta (Betta), the page advises not feeding them for a day, then viewing 4–5 fish in a glass jar under light: males have pointed heads, flat bellies and longer fins; females have tapered heads, plump striped bellies and neat fins.
Sex betta (Betta) in good light, using a torch on the tank, rather than in a dark setting.
For breeding guppies (Poecilia reticulata), keep 1 male to 2 to 3 females.
Female guppies (Poecilia reticulata) give birth about every 30 days and will eat their own young unless the fry have plenty of hiding places.
For species hard to sex, such as cyprinids and tetras, buy a small group to be more likely to get a pair.
Male betta (Betta) build bubble nests and should be kept apart until ready to breed; remove the female after spawning so she is not attacked.
General sexing rules for cichlids (Cichlidae) may not apply to every species, so research the species before pairing fish to breed.
Information on sexing fish can also be got from a veterinarian, books, hobby magazines or the internet.
Do not rely on any single feature to sex betta (Betta); combine several features.
Even long-time betta (Betta) keepers often sort males and females wrongly; the signs are relative comparisons, not absolute rules.
Male betta (Betta) become aggressive and chase each other when two males meet.
Male guppies (Poecilia reticulata) sometimes behave aggressively towards each other.
The page claims betta (Betta) have both male and female sex organs; this is not supported, as betta have separate sexes.
Hybrids of guppies (Poecilia reticulata) with other Poecilia species are always male and appear to be sterile.
